scenes.narration: The self that experiences Logotherapy is a committee, not a king. Logotherapy is a form of existential therapy developed by neurologist and psychiatrist Viktor Frankl. It is founded on the premise that the primary motivational force of individuals is to find meaning in life.

Reproduction explains more of Logotherapy than any philosophy dares to admit. Frankl describes it as "the Third Viennese School of Psychotherapy" along with Freud's psychoanalysis and Alfred Adler's individual psychology. Logotherapy is based on an existential analysis focusing on Kierkegaard's will to meaning as opposed to Adler's Nietzschean doctrine of will to power or Freud's will to pleasure.

Once you see Logotherapy as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. Rather than power or pleasure, logotherapy is founded upon the belief that striving to find meaning in life is the primary, most powerful motivating and driving force in humans. A short introduction to this system is given in Frankl's most famous book, Man's Search for Meaning (1946), in which he outlines how his theories helped him to survive his Holocaust experience and how that experience further developed and reinforced his theories.

The story Logotherapy tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. The notion of logotherapy was created with the Greek word logos ("meaning"). Frankl's concept is based on the premise that the primary motivational force of an individual is to find meaning in life.

Meaning is not found in Logotherapy — it is manufactured for it. We have freedom to find meaning in what we do, and what we experience, or at least in the stance we take when faced with a situation of unchangeable suffering. The human spirit is referred to in several of the assumptions of logotherapy, but the use of the term spirit is not "spiritual" or "religious." In Frankl's view, the spirit is the will of the human being.

The cold light on Logotherapy leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. The emphasis, therefore, is on the search for meaning, which is not necessarily the search for God or any other supernatural being. Frankl also noted the barriers to humanity's quest for meaning in life.

Logotherapy did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. Purpose in life and meaning in life constructs appeared in Frankl's logotherapy writings with relation to existential vacuum and will to meaning, as well as others who have theorized about and defined positive psychological functioning. Frankl observed that it may be psychologically damaging when a person's search for meaning is blocked.

The honest version of Logotherapy starts by giving up the comforting part. Positive life purpose and meaning were associated with strong religious beliefs, membership in groups, dedication to a cause, life values, and clear goals. Maturity emphasizes a clear comprehension of life's purpose, directedness, and intentionality which contributes to the feeling that life is meaningful.

Strip Logotherapy of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Furthermore, Frankl’s (2006) theory also supports that logotherapy can help individuals discover meaning in their lives, leading to increased self-confidence and happiness. Frankl's ideas were operationalized by Crumbaugh and Maholick's Purpose in Life (PIL) test, which measures an individual's meaning and purpose in life.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Logotherapy shows exactly where that breaks. With the test, investigators found that meaning in life mediated the relationships between religiosity and well-being; uncontrollable stress and substance use; depression and self-derogation. Crumbaugh found that the Seeking of Noetic Goals Test (SONG) is a complementary measure of the PIL.

What looks like free choice in Logotherapy is older than choice itself. While the PIL measures the presence of meaning, the SONG measures orientation towards meaning. A low score in the PIL but a high score in the SONG, would predict a better outcome in the application of Logotherapy.

Nobody designed the part of Logotherapy you experience — it was inherited. He could not overcome the loss of his wife who had died two years before and whom he had loved above all else. Frankl emphasized that realizing the value of suffering is meaningful only when the first two creative possibilities are not available (for example, in a concentration camp) and only when such suffering is inevitable – he was not proposing that people suffer unnecessarily.

Every serious account of Logotherapy eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Frankl described the meta-clinical implications of logotherapy in his book The Will to Meaning: Foundations and Applications of Logotherapy. As an existential psychologist, he inherently disagreed with the "machine model" or "rat model", as it undermines the human quality of humans.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Logotherapy — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. As a neurologist and psychiatrist, Frankl developed a unique view of determinism to coexist with the three basic pillars of logotherapy (the freedom of will). In doing such, a person can detach from situations and themselves, choose an attitude about themselves, and determine their own determinants, thus shaping their own character and becoming responsible for themselves.

The selfish-gene reading of Logotherapy makes it less romantic and far more precise. Anecdotes about this use of logotherapy are given by New York Times writer Tim Sanders, who explained how he uses its concept to relieve the stress of fellow airline travelers by asking them the purpose of their journey. When he does this, no matter how miserable they are, their whole demeanor changes, and they remain happy throughout the flight.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. Overall, Frankl believed that the anxious individual does not understand that their anxiety is the result of dealing with a sense of "unfulfilled responsibility" and ultimately a lack of meaning. Frankl cites two neurotic pathogens: hyper-intention, a forced intention toward some end which makes that end unattainable; and hyper-reflection, an excessive attention to oneself which stifles attempts to avoid the neurosis to which one thinks oneself predisposed.

The feeling that Logotherapy means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. Frankl identified anticipatory anxiety, a fear of a given outcome which makes that outcome more likely. To relieve the anticipatory anxiety and treat the resulting neuroses, logotherapy offers paradoxical intention, wherein the patient intends to do the opposite of their hyper-intended goal.

Nothing in Logotherapy was built for you — it was built for reproduction. A person, then, who fears (i.e. experiences anticipatory anxiety over) not getting a good night's sleep may try too hard (that is, hyper-intend) to fall asleep, and this would hinder their ability to do so. A logotherapist would recommend, then, that the person go to bed and intentionally try not to fall asleep.

The psychology underneath Logotherapy is simpler and older than the story on top. This would relieve the anticipatory anxiety which kept the person awake in the first place, thus allowing them to fall asleep in an acceptable amount of time. Viktor Frankl believed depression occurred at the psychological, physiological, and spiritual levels.

Behind Logotherapy sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. At the psychological level, he believed that feelings of inadequacy stem from undertaking tasks beyond our abilities. At the physiological level, he recognized a "vital low", which he defined as a "diminishment of physical energy".

The nihilist does not deny Logotherapy — he only refuses to flatter it. Finally, Frankl believed that at the spiritual level, the depressed individual faces tension between who they actually are in relation to what they should be. Finally Frankl suggests that if goals seem unreachable, an individual loses a sense of future and thus meaning, resulting in depression.

What culture calls destiny in Logotherapy is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. Thus logotherapy aims "to change the patient's attitude toward their disease as well as toward their life as a task". In order to overcome depressed feelings and thoughts, Frankl challenges individuals who have depression to find meaning in their suffering.

The genes do not care about Logotherapy; they care about copies. Frankl frequently cites Nietzsche's words, "If we have our own why in life, we shall get along with almost any how". Suffering and all the negative emotions that come with it are a normal part of the human experience and should even be expected.

Take away the meaning and Logotherapy still functions — that is the disturbing part. Frankl believed that those with obsessive–compulsive disorder lack the sense of completion that most other individuals possess. Therefore, it is important to recognize that the patient is "not responsible for his obsessional ideas", but that "he is certainly responsible for his attitude toward these ideas".

The unconscious does not argue with Logotherapy; it simply acts first. Frankl suggested that it is important for the patient to recognize their inclinations toward perfection as fate, and therefore, must learn to accept some degrees of uncertainty. Ultimately, following the premise of logotherapy, the patient must eventually ignore their obsessional thoughts and find meaning in their life despite such thoughts.

Logotherapy feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Though logotherapy was not intended to deal with severe disorders, Frankl believed that logotherapy could benefit even those with schizophrenia. In this dysfunction, the person with schizophrenia "experiences himself as an object" rather than as a subject.

The bleak reading of Logotherapy is also the most testable one. Frankl suggested that a person with schizophrenia could be helped by logotherapy by first being taught to ignore voices and to end persistent self-observation. In 1977, Terry Zuehlke and John Watkins conducted a study analyzing the effectiveness of logotherapy in treating terminally ill patients.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Logotherapy. The study's design used 20 male Veterans Administration volunteers who were randomly assigned to one of two possible treatments – (1) group that received eight 45-minute sessions over a 2-week period and (2) group used as control that received delayed treatment. Each group was tested on five scales – the MMPI K Scale, MMPI L Scale, Death Anxiety Scale, Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale, and the Purpose of Life Test.

The self that experiences Logotherapy is a committee, not a king. The results showed an overall significant difference between the control and treatment groups. While the univariate analyses showed that there were significant group differences in 3/5 of the dependent measures.

Reproduction explains more of Logotherapy than any philosophy dares to admit. These results confirm the idea that terminally ill patients can benefit from logotherapy in coping with death. It requires of the therapist to note the innate strengths that people have and how they have dealt with adversity and suffering in life; to ask the patient to consider how, despite everything a person may have gone through, they made the best of their suffering.

The method is called "Ecce Homo", which is Latin for "Behold the Man", because the method involves beholding how other people have made the best of their adversity. Frankl explicitly replied to May's arguments through a written dialogue, sparked by Rabbi Reuven Bulka's article "Is Logotherapy Authoritarian?".

Frankl responded that he combined the prescription of medication, if necessary, with logotherapy, to deal with the person's psychological and emotional reaction to the illness, and highlighted areas of freedom and responsibility, where the person is free to search and to find meaning.
